title: HeatWave Audit Center — OCI Streaming demonstration
mode: Illustrative replay; application templates with isolated fixture data. No live source mutations or OCI delivery claims.

scenes.title: Every row has a story
scenes.narration: Welcome to HeatWave Audit Center. Source left, controls in the centre, audit history right. This walkthrough uses illustrative demo data.
scenes.caption: Source → OCI Streaming → retained audit history

scenes.title: Safe harbor statement
scenes.narration: This demonstration explains the current application and its limits. Oracle styling does not imply Oracle authorship or endorsement. The security audit extension shown later is not implemented in this application.
scenes.caption: Information only · Current capabilities and extension boundaries are identified
scenes.text: The following is intended to outline our general product direction. It is intended for information purposes only, and may not be incorporated into any contract. It is not a commitment to deliver any material, code, or functionality, and should not be relied upon in making purchasing decisions. The development, release, timing, and pricing of any features or functionality described for Oracle’s products may change and remains at the sole discretion of Oracle Corporation.

scenes.title: One compartment. One traceable data path.
scenes.narration: The web application runs on Oracle Linux nine. Debezium and the history writer run on O C I Container Instances. Debezium reads source changes, publishes to O C I Streaming, and the writer commits history to the target. Vault holds credentials. Resource access stays in the virtual machine compartment.
scenes.caption: OL9 control plane · OCI Container Instances · OCI Streaming · HeatWave target

scenes.title: Create a table with a stable row key
scenes.narration: Begin with a demo orders table and a primary key. Creating this table prepares the source before registration. Because capture starts later, its first schema observation is a baseline. It is not a claim that the earlier create statement was captured from the binary log.
scenes.caption: CREATE TABLE before capture → schema baseline at initialization
scenes.source:
CREATE TABLE demo_sales.orders (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
    DEFAULT 'new',
  amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
    DEFAULT 0.00
);

scenes.title: Connect, discover and register
scenes.narration: Register the source and target connections. The Test connection button checks MySQL access using a Vault secret reference. Table mappings load schemas and tables from those connections. Select one registration and choose Edit to change its available settings. Existing capture identities remain protected.
scenes.caption: Test connection → discover objects → map source to audit target

scenes.title: Select OCI Streaming resources
scenes.narration: Create or select a stream pool, a data stream, and a Connect configuration. Add a queue connection using principal authentication. The mapping uses the data stream; its separate schema stream must also be ready. This demonstration uses O C I Streaming throughout.
scenes.caption: Data stream: demo-orders · Schema stream: audit_1 · Principal authentication

scenes.title: Start from now, then verify delivery
scenes.narration: A new flow initialized at End captures schema and future changes, without copying existing rows. Restarts resume saved offsets. Verify messages and target events, not just container status.
scenes.caption: New flow: End = no existing-row snapshot · Restart = saved checkpoint

scenes.title: INSERT → CREATE with an AFTER image
scenes.narration: Insert order ten forty two. Debezium represents the insert as a create event. Its before image is null; its after image contains the new row. The writer stores the key, source position, queue offset and images. A successful target commit must precede acknowledgement of the message.
scenes.caption: CREATE: BEFORE = null · AFTER = inserted row
scenes.source:
INSERT INTO demo_sales.orders
  (id, status, amount)
VALUES
  (1042, 'new', 80.00);

scenes.title: UPDATE → compare complete images
scenes.narration: Now change the order status and amount. The same key links the earlier and later versions. Select the update in Change history, then Compare images. The before image shows new and eighty; the after image shows paid and ninety nine point ninety five. Full row images require the correct source settings.
scenes.caption: UPDATE: new / 80.00 → paid / 99.95 · binlog_row_image = FULL
scenes.source:
UPDATE demo_sales.orders
SET status = 'paid',
    amount = 99.95
WHERE id = 1042;

scenes.title: DELETE → retain the final BEFORE image
scenes.narration: Delete the source row. It disappears from the current source table, but the audit record retains its final before image. The after image is null. History remains available for the original insert, the update and the deletion. Deleting source data does not erase audit history.
scenes.caption: DELETE: BEFORE = final row · AFTER = null · History remains

scenes.title: Find one row across its lifetime
scenes.narration: Search with the typed record key, id ten forty two, and a retained date range. The application computes the same keyed fingerprint from the source identity, schema, table and key. An indexed lookup finds that row’s changes. Separate image fingerprints describe content changes; the event identity supports replay deduplication.
scenes.caption: Typed key → stable key fingerprint → indexed, time-bounded history

scenes.title: DDL → compare the table structure
scenes.narration: Add a region column with a default, and widen the amount type. Schema events use the separate schema stream. The target stores the prior definition, new definition and a semantic difference. Here, SQL inspection shows the new column and decimal precision change. Defaults, indexes and partitions can only be compared when the captured metadata contains them. Unknown properties stay unknown.
scenes.caption: Separate schema history · Compare captured properties · Unknown stays unknown
scenes.source:
ALTER TABLE demo_sales.orders
  ADD COLUMN region VARCHAR(16)
    DEFAULT 'EMEA',
  MODIFY amount DECIMAL(14,2)
    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00;

scenes.title: Users and privileges need security evidence
scenes.narration: Create a locked demonstration user, grant select, then revoke it. These are account and privilege operations, not row updates. This application does not yet collect them as a security history. Use the MySQL Enterprise Audit plugin with reviewed filters and a separate collector. Retain the actor, account, scope, action, outcome and timestamp. Do not infer complete privilege history from row change capture.
scenes.caption: DCL extension is not implemented · Use database audit logs and a separate collector

scenes.title: From all databases to one table
scenes.narration: The Audit Center opens with all databases. A pie chart compares event counts. Choose a database slice or its legend entry to see registered table bars, then select a table to drill into changes over time. These overview counts are a separate sample dataset, not the three earlier demonstration transactions.
scenes.caption: All databases pie → database table bars → table changes over time

scenes.title: Choose the interval, range and chart
scenes.narration: Choose a custom date range and an interval of minute, hour, day or week. Minute charts cover one hour. Switch between line, bar and stacked bar, and use the operation legend. Counts include snapshots unless you filter them out. Download a chart image or export the loaded table data.
scenes.caption: Custom UTC range · Minute / Hour / Day / Week · Line / Bar / Stacked bar

scenes.title: Rows, structures and security: clear boundaries
scenes.narration: Capture row images, compare schemas, and explore history and charts. Security auditing needs a separate collector. This was an illustrative replay.
scenes.caption: Row history + schema evidence + charts · Security collector remains a separate extension
